item.title: Why Linux never needed defragging, while Windows relied on it for decades
item.itunes:title: Why Linux never needed defragging, while Windows relied on it for decades
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you used Windows back in the day, you probably remember whittling away the days watching the colorful defragmentation tool work away to help speed up your disk reads. And while the introduction of SSDs and automatic organization services in Windows has generally reduced the need to run the defragger (if at all), it's still a cool chapter in how we used our PCs back then.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But when was the last time you defragged a Linux machine, even if it wasn't running off an SSD? There's a good chance you haven't; in fact, it's totally reasonable that a regular Linux user never feels the need to. And that difference shows how Windows grew up.

Microsoft's architecture dates back to 1977

Back when Microsoft was chewing the FAT

So, how come Windows on an HDD needs defragging to stay responsive, but Linux doesn't? Well, Microsoft's OS has quite a few more years on Team Tux. Back in 1977, Microsoft invented the File Allocation Table (FAT), which was designed for fitting data onto floppy disks. Floppies were quite tight on space (they were around 100 KB at the time), so FAT had to use some smart tactics to squeeze everything on.

Fitting everything on was like trying to pack a tight suitcase. Everything was assigned a block and occupied that block. When a small block was deleted and a large block was added, the system couldn't afford to ignore that little block.

To help fill the gap and keep as much space open as possible, the system would take a chunk out of the large block, put it into the smaller space, and then place the rest at the end. It helped save space, but now reading that one large block requires two reads from different locations, slowing things down.

Things got weird when a block grew, usually because more data had been added. If another block had been positioned next to it by then, FAT would have to take the new block and place it somewhere else, further fragmenting the data on the drive.

Defragging's goal was to sort all these blocks so that there were no breaks between them. It took a little bit of time to shuffle those blocks around, but once it was done, reading files got noticeably faster.

Windows still asks about this floppy-era setting every time you format a drive

A 30-year-old Windows NT setting has persisted to this day

1
By  Tanveer Singh

Linux had the benefit of starting with Unix mentalities

It didn't need to squish data onto a floppy disk

14 years after Microsoft used FAT on floppy disks, Linux entered the scene. Its inventor, Linus Torvalds, was inspired by the Unix OS when he attended the University of Helsinki. He wanted to work on operating systems at home, so he grabbed a copy of MINIX, an OS that existed to teach people how to code for operating systems. It wasn't based on Unix, but it was 'Unix-like', so it was a good fit.

When Torvalds then moved on to making Linux, he took the Unix mentality and worked with it. Linux developers, specifically Rémy Card, designed a new format for the OS called 'ext'. This didn't use the same 'tight suitcase' storage method as FAT; its data architecture was more like islands. Each block was separate from the others and had room to "grow", so if anything new developed, it could just take new space without having to split the block into smaller pieces.

Linux isn't totally free of the need for defragmentation, though. If you have minimal free space on a drive, or you download lots of gigabyte-sized files in small, randomized chunks, you may need to give your system a defrag to get things working smoothly again. But for regular use, the ext format didn't need defragging.

My Linux desktop fits on a USB drive, and it boots the same on any PC I use

My full setup, wherever I go

12
By  João Carrasqueira

Linux not needing a defrag isn't as strong a bonus as it once was

Defragging isn't really needed these days

Of course, this all implies that people run defraggers in the first place. With SSDs becoming affordable and people using them as primary drives for the OS and software, defragging falls out of the picture. In fact, it's highly recommended you never defrag an SSD, because the damage you do from the intense write actions supersedes the benefits you get from defragging. After all, fragmentation was a problem back when data drives (like HDDs) had moving parts that needed to physically seek out blocks of data. SSDs have no moving parts, so they have no seek time.

However, the fact that Linux didn't need it nearly as much as Windows is a cool insight into how both operating systems started and how they grew. Microsoft didn't have the luxury to wait a decade or two before it jumped into the OS world; it had to work with what it had at the time. Meanwhile, Linus Torvalds could pick the foundation that suited his project, and that meant no defrags.

I enabled Windows 11's drive compression and got over 60GB back without slowing down my PC

This should be more obvious

11
By  João Carrasqueira

Linux didn't need the same floppy disk tech as Microsoft

While disk defragging is not nearly the mainstay maintenance tool as it once was, the story behind why Windows needed it, and Linux didn't, is pretty interesting. Regardless, I don't miss those long defrag days; I'll stick to SSDs, thanks.

item.title: I tested the 3 Claude Code alternatives the internet keeps talking about, and only one let me down
item.itunes:title: I tested the 3 Claude Code alternatives the internet keeps talking about, and only one let me down
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It seems as though every week, a new thread on Reddit or a YouTube short on my feed tells me that I'm overpaying for Claude Code, and that it's finally time to move on from weekly and 5-hour usage limits. Every time, it's purported that either a rival or a free coding agent can do a better job, and Codex, Antigravity, and OpenCode come up in nearly all of those conversations.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I decided that it was about time to stop listening to the discourse and give all three a job I would normally hand off to Claude Code without a second thought. The task was to build a utility that I use almost every other week to organize my benchmarking data which works fully offline, flags the fastest runs, and lets me compare any two runs for performance variance. Here's how I ran the test, and what I found.

The task was to make my benchmarking experience easier

A single HTML file that organizes my data and works fully offline

One of the reasons why I chose this specific tool to build is because my workflow involves running and logging benchmarks every other week. Doing so manually means opening up a spreadsheet, populating the rows and columns for the title's name, the specific preset I chose, average FPS for each run, the fastest result for every game per given preset, and the percentage gap between any two runs.

Every tool I tested got the same prompt in an empty folder with one attempt to build the utility, with no follow-ups, hand holding, or remedial prompts. Codex and Antigravity ran the best models their free tiers offer, GPT-5.6 Terra and Gemini 3.8 Flash, both set to high. Claude Code has no free tier, but for consistency, I ran it on Sonnet 5.5, the model Anthropic gives free users in chat, also set to high. OpenCode on the other hand, ran Qwen3.6-35B-A3B locally on my RTX 4070 Ti Super.

I gave the following prompt to all three:

Build me a benchmark run logger as a single HTML file I can open by double-clicking it in my browser. It must work with no accounts, no server, and no internet connection, saving everything in the browser itself. I can type in a game name, a settings preset, and an average FPS for each run. It shows my runs in a list and highlights the fastest run for each game. When I select two runs, it shows the percentage difference, using the first run I selected as the baseline. I can delete a run. The list should still be there after I refresh the page.

Once the generation was completed, I devised the following criteria for evaluation.

Check

What I tested

Adding runs

Can a game, a preset, and average FPS be logged?

Fastest run

Is the highest FPS run for each game highlighted?

Baseline

Is the first run clicked the baseline?

Deleting

Can a run be removed from the list?

Saving

Do all runs remain after a page refresh?

Self-check

Did the tool test its own work before the handoff?
I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

OpenCode built a lean and clean logger, with one issue

It picked the wrong baseline every time, and it changes things

OpenCode's run is a little different from the rest, especially given that I'm running the stack on my hardware. It ran Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at UD-IQ4_XS, served through llama.cpp on my RTX 4070 Ti Super with a 64K context window and Qwen's recommended samplers for coding tasks.

The model thought for about 1 minute and 42 seconds and produced a lean, clean, and fully offline logger that passed four of the six criteria, but slipped on the math on the baseline. When I clicked the 120 FPS run first, it still treated the lower of the two (100 FPS) as the baseline and reported a 20% gain instead of a drop of 16.7%.

It turns out the issue was the model choosing the baseline by position on the list rather than my click selection. My first quick test missed this one entirely because it shows up only for certain combinations of entry and click order, which makes the issue difficult to diagnose if you're not putting the output and behavior under the microscope like I did.

I switched to Claude Code's open-source rival and stopped worrying about rate limits

It's not about escaping Claude, it's about escaping counting

23
By  Nolen Jonker

Antigravity over-engineered, but I'm not complaining

Gemini 3.8 Flash delivered the most stunning interface of the lot

Gemini 3.8 Flash's HTML tool arrived with an interface that was certainly dressed to impress, and if you're as much of a geek when it comes to impressive user interfaces as I am, you'd have chosen your winner at this step already. What's even better is the fact that the functionality itself wasn't lacking in any department, and the output passed all the six checks on the first attempt. Then, however, the model decided to keep going, and took three minutes to finish. For some context, 3.8 Flash's file ran to 1,976 lines, nearly five times the roughly 400-line average of the other three.

The logger suggests game titles and common graphical presets as I type, and it adds search, game filters, sorting, and a stats bar, plus frame-times in every comparison. There's also a "Swap Roles" button that flips the baseline with a single click, which makes benchmarking less of a cognitive load-inducing activity.

The most impressive aspect came as a surprise. It also checked its own work before handing it over, which I discovered later as I went through the reasoning. It ran a syntax check and set of logic tests on the file, which is more than what Codex did. What it didn't resist was going further than asked by writing the file and copying it to a mirrored version for good measure, which made it take slightly longer than Claude Code or Codex to finish. For a free model, that's highly impressive.

I replaced my VS Code workflow with Google Antigravity, and cut my coding time in half

Building complex projects no longer feels exhausting.

12
By  Parth Shah

Codex came closest to Claude Code

GPT-5.6 Terra was the closest match on utility

Codex was running GPT-5.6 Terra on high under the hood, and it finished generation in a total of 2 minutes and 42 seconds. Claude Code, on the other hand, took 2 minutes and 14 seconds, and passed all six checks on the first attempt. The response was rather characteristic of GPT, in that it delivered exactly what the prompt asked for, and nothing else.

The HTML labels the baseline, spells out the result as a sentence, and saves all that data offline. GPT-5.6 Terra also ran a syntax check on the file before handing it over. Where it did fall short of Claude Code is depth, since Sonnet 5.5 tested the page in a browser, while Codex never bothered to open it.

Two free models matched Claude Code, and that's a pleasant surprise

If you've gone through any of these model benchmarks in the last few months, you probably already expected Claude to take the crown outright when it comes to coding capabilities, because, after all, its flagship models lead most specialized agentic coding tests today. I would steer away from a decisive verdict based on one test, but it finally feels as though for everyday coding tasks for the average user, that gap may not be a metaphorical chasm anymore.

Adding runs

item.title: I tried 4 open-source Google Maps alternatives, and one was an easy winner
item.itunes:title: I tried 4 open-source Google Maps alternatives, and one was an easy winner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Google Maps is convenient, but it's not the only way to get around. If you want more privacy, fewer distractions, or a change of pace, open-source mapping apps are worth exploring. I tried four options to see how they compare and what each brings to the table.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

From feature-packed navigation tools to apps designed for outdoor adventures, they approach mapping in different ways. I wanted something practical for everyday use, not an app that takes ages to figure out. One of these Google Maps alternatives stood out for all the right reasons.

CoMaps

A clean mapping app with privacy in mind

CoMaps caught my attention because it takes a community-driven approach to navigation. Contributors built it to keep mapping tools open, privacy-friendly, and accessible to everyone. I found that background interesting because it gives the app a clear purpose beyond simply offering another way to get directions.

The interface feels familiar if you've used other OpenStreetMap-based apps, so I didn't have to spend much time figuring out how to use it. I could explore places, look up destinations, and plan trips without dealing with a cluttered interface. The app also supports offline maps, which makes it practical for traveling through areas where mobile connectivity isn't reliable.

The project emphasizes transparency and gives users an alternative to navigation apps built around advertising and data collection. However, it is still worth checking whether its current features and map coverage meet your needs before making the switch. I see CoMaps as a promising option, particularly for people who value open-source software and want more control over their digital tools.

CoMaps
See at Google Play Store
4 Waze alternatives that give me Android Auto navigation without the privacy baggage

Offline navigation finally works better than Waze, and these apps prove it

By  Dhruv Bhutani

Trail Sense

A smarter way to explore remote trails

For outdoor adventures, I found Trail Sense useful because it helps me navigate and stay aware of my surroundings without relying on an internet connection. It's designed for hiking and other outdoor activities, where having access to useful information can make a real difference.

The app uses sensors built into my phone to provide tools such as a compass, altimeter, and location tracking. It also includes features that help me estimate the sun's position, monitor weather conditions, and find my way when exploring unfamiliar trails. I liked that many of these tools work offline, making the app practical for places where mobile signals are unreliable.

What stood out to me was its focus on outdoor safety rather than everyday commuting. I could see it being useful for hikers, campers, and anyone who enjoys exploring remote locations. However, its feature set is geared toward outdoor activities so that it won't suit every navigation need. For me, Trail Sense is a handy addition to an outdoor toolkit, especially when I want useful navigation and environmental information available directly on my phone.

Trail Sense
See at Google Play Store

OsmAnd

A feature-packed map with a learning curve

OsmAnd is the app I would turn to when basic navigation isn't enough. Compared with simpler mapping apps, it offers a lot more control over how I explore places and plan routes. At first, the number of options felt a little overwhelming, but I could see why people who enjoy outdoor adventures might appreciate the extra detail.

What stood out to me was the level of information available on the map. I could explore terrain, view contour lines, and access details useful for planning hiking or cycling routes. OsmAnd also supports GPX tracks, which makes it easier to follow a planned route or keep track of a journey. I liked that I could customize the map and navigation settings to suit different activities instead of relying on one fixed experience.

However, all these features come with a learning curve. The interface isn't as straightforward as I'd like for quick, everyday trips, and some features require a paid plan. I think OsmAnd makes the most sense for people who want detailed maps and advanced navigation controls rather than a simple, no-fuss replacement for Google Maps.

OsmAnd
See at Google Play Store

Organic Maps

A Google Maps alternative without the clutter

What I appreciated about Organic Maps was how much control it gave me over my maps without complicating the experience. I could customize map details, save bookmarks into folders, and import or export GPX and KML files to organize my trips. These options were especially useful when planning multiple stops or grouping places by destination.

I also liked that I could download individual regions instead of depending on a constant internet connection. The app supports offline search and navigation, so I could still find saved places and explore downloaded maps while traveling. Its ability to display useful details such as hiking paths, cycling routes, and points of interest made it suitable for more than just driving around town.

The best part was the absence of ads, tracking, and mandatory account sign-ins. I didn't have to build my experience around a Google account or share my location with an advertising ecosystem to use the core features. Google Maps offers more connected services, but Organic Maps gives me a simpler, more independent way to manage navigation. I could tailor the map to my needs without unnecessary distractions.

Organic Maps
See at Google Play Store
I tried to ditch Google Maps, but these 5 features kept pulling me back

Replacing Google Maps is easy until you realize how many little things you actually rely on.

By  Yash Patel

My Google Maps replacement is simpler than I expected

After trying all four apps, I realized that switching away from Google Maps doesn't mean compromising on navigation. Each tool offers something different, but Organic Maps struck the right balance for my everyday needs. I liked its straightforward approach without unnecessary distractions. With Organic Maps, you might find that you need Google Maps less than you thought.

item.title: Voice control is the worst way to start a smart home, but it's how nearly everyone starts
item.itunes:title: Voice control is the worst way to start a smart home, but it's how nearly everyone starts
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a lot of people, the typical smart home journey begins with a holiday sale smart speaker, like an Echo Dot or a Google Nest Mini, plugged into a kitchen counter, followed by shouting, "Alexa, turn on the living room lights." Voice assistants offer an accessible low-friction onboarding experience for so many users. But treating voice as the primary control mechanism for an entire household quickly introduces latency, privacy compromises, and domestic friction. Voice control makes a terrible primary automation layer. Building a reliable high-performance smart home requires prioritizing local deterministic inputs (such as physical switches, presence detection, and automated triggers) while relegating voice to a secondary fallback route.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
I swapped my Google Nest Mini for a self-hosted open-source voice assistant, and it’s brilliant

The Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition has been a very interesting journey so far.

5
By  Adam Conway

Voice control should not be the basis of your smart home

Save it for your weird queries

Why does voice control fail so largely as an architecture? Voice-first setups are fragile, and voice commands are rarely processed locally. When you're picking up cheap consumer speakers, for the budget entry-level endpoints, audio files must be streamed to cloud servers like AWS for Alexa or Google Cloud for the Google Home products. They must then be passed to remote natural language processing models, matched against cloud-hosted device states, and routed back down via API calls. This introduces multi-second delays compared to local execution.

Voice-centric architecture introduces a critical single point of failure because you're depending on the internet. If your broadband connection drops or a regional cloud outage hits, your entire home automation interface grinds to a halt. A local switch shouldn't stop working just because an external DNS server is struggling.

It can also lead to a lot of domestic friction with other members of your household. Shouting commands across a room is socially awkward, disruptive during late-night hours, and unnatural compared to flipping a physical switch or letting automation handle the environment silently.

Local automation is the basis of the true smart home

Make your home work for you

When you switch to local automation paired with physical inputs, you get rid of many of the problems outlined above because these devices operate entirely over local network transports. You will never have to contact an off-site server with your smart home. This means state changes execute instantly, consistently achieving sub-100ms response times. It can feel like it's recreated the immediate zero-lag tactile feel of a traditional hardwired wall switch, eliminating that multi-second delay that disrupts a lot of basic home interaction with voice control.

Alongside this, you're no longer dependent on an internet connection for your architecture to actually work. Local automation with physical inputs operates on local-first architecture, where the device state machines, automation scripts, and routing tables all run on an on-premises host like a dedicated mini PC or home server. This means you still get full operational integrity even if the WAN fiber connection is completely cut or any upstream DNS servers fail. It guarantees zero-downtime household infrastructure, insulating critical lighting, heating, and access controls from external ISP or cloud platform failures.

Finally, local execution preserves strict data privacy. All of your telemetry, sensor logs, and operational states remain strictly on-premises on local storage media, never leaving your private network segment. You don't have to worry about your information being accessed by outside sources. It restores absolute operational predictability while completely eliminating off-premises telemetry streaming, keeping raw household behavioral data under local ownership.

Build a better smart home

Voice commands should not be important

If you want to create a resilient smart home, then the way it should be constructed is by building from the infrastructure up rather than building around a cheap voice-controlled hub. Establish a local control layer first. Deploy a local orchestration platform like Home Assistant running on containerized hardware or a dedicated mini PC rather than relying on third-party manufacturer apps tied to cloud bridges.

Next, fix the physical control layer. You can deploy smart switches or smart buttons that maintain power to the circuit while sending discrete local signals, or use a decoupled smart bulb binding so physical wall switches never leave dead zones.

The true way to create a home that really feels smart is by automating the environment around you. You can implement presence detection through mmWave radars or Bluetooth proxies, as well as time-of-day logic, so lights and climate controls adjust automatically without requiring any active human input.

You should treat voice commands as an edge case. Retain those voice assistants solely for abstract queries, timers, or edge case overrides rather than routing core environmental controls through a cloud microphone.

A true smart home doesn't rely on voice commands

Local control is the way forward

Voice control lowers the barrier to entry when it comes to smart home products, but it scales poorly as your home actually grows. Stop designing your smart home around what you can shout across a room. Instead, build a deterministic local automation foundation that reacts to presence and physical input, and let your house run itself quietly in the background.

You get your Jellyfin instance up and running with your favorite shows and movies, your Immich library up as a Google Photos replacement, maybe a few other experimental containers. Then you leave the house and attempt to access them while on public Wi-Fi or cellular, and nothing loads.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For many self-hosters, remote access is seen as the last hurdle or "final boss" of their setup, and that checks out when you parse through all the different advice that gets passed around. Port forward this, never port forward that, VPN here, WireGuard there—it can make your head spin if you're new. Even as someone who knows their way around home networking, NetBird simplified everything to a few copy-pasted commands and client installations, and my services were accessible from everywhere within minutes.

3
By  Ty Sherback

Getting a private network running shouldn't take a weekend

NetBird made it incredibly simple

NetBird's standard cloud-based deployment is about as close to "a few clicks" as a mesh VPN can get. You create an account, install the client on the machine running your services along with anything else you intend to use to access them, and then sign in on each of those. After that, you're basically done. The devices appear on the dashboard with addresses on a private range that they reach each other through, and it doesn't take forwarding any ports or writing configs by hand.

The reason why it works so quickly and reliably is the same reason why other services like Tailscale also work so well. NetBird builds a mesh on top of WireGuard and uses ICE, which is a NAT traversal technique that finds direct paths between two devices. If a path can't be found, it falls back to a relay server that NetBird runs, which keeps your services accessible even in cases where port forwarding isn't possible. That traffic is also encrypted end-to-end, so virtually no privacy risk here.

After getting online, everything was accessible immediately. I could browse and backup my Immich library, stream from Jellyfin, and even SSH into any part of my home lab that the client was installed on. The dashboard also lets you sort devices and users into groups with custom access policies, which is useful if you plan to have anyone besides you logging on.

Is Tailscale the safest way to access your home network remotely?

Tailscale is easy to set up, but is that trading off your security?

By  Joe Rice-Jones

NetBird covers public access, too

All without opening a port

Private access solves the problem for you and anyone in your immediate circle, but plenty of home labs host things for other people. I run TeamSpeak and game servers for friends, and while I could ask everyone to install a VPN client to join up, I doubt I'd have many takers. Those services were the reason I relied on port forwarding, until I moved house. My new ISP stuck me behind CGNAT, which basically closed that door on me for good.

NetBird's integrated reverse proxy opens that door again. You can create the service you wish to host through the dashboard, and NetBird will provision a public domain with TLS automatically. Incoming traffic will hit NetBird's proxy cluster, which then forwards it through an encrypted tunnel to your machine running the service—no port forwarding required. On the standard cloud deployment, you can use a free domain on NetBird's shared proxy infrastructure, or bring your own. NetBird also adds the ability to lock the services behind SSO, a PIN, or a standard password, which is great for web-based services.

A standard reverse proxy setup that most home lab users deploy won't work with layer 4 TCP and UDP services like the aforementioned VOIP and game server, but NetBird has you covered here too. You can expose these through the same cluster, but because they're layer 4 services, you can't put SSO, password, or PIN protection on them, so the security is only as good as the service itself allows.

5
By  Rich Edmonds

The convenience comes with trade-offs

You're trusting an external service

On NetBird Cloud, NetBird’s management service registers your devices, distributes keys, and enforces your policies. It never carries your traffic, which flows directly between devices or through a relay that can’t decrypt it. If that service goes down, existing connections will be fine but you won't be able to tweak them or add new ones until it's back.

There's also potential for friction across devices that don't support the NetBird client, which admittedly isn't many, but it's something to consider. Relayed connections might keep things working in the event something drops out, but they add latency and share the relay’s bandwidth, and you can feel that when streaming. Abstraction can cut both ways, too: when my Immich access stalled over DNS resolution and NetBird’s lazy connection setting, tracking it down took far longer than the original setup did, but that's the price of admission.

There are a lot of different ways to access your self-hosted services when away, but here's what works for me.

9
By  Adam Conway

Self-hosting NetBird answers most of these objections

You can host the same control plane, and it's completely free and open-source

If you're like many home lab enthusiasts, you've probably developed a healthy distrust of putting part of your home infrastructure in the hands of a company, but NetBird addresses that, too. NetBird’s entire control plane is open source and self-hostable, which is where I ended up. Moving off Cloud doesn't change how I use my devices or how the control-plane functions, it just changes which server they phone home to.

It’s also far more approachable than self-hosting a VPN used to be. NetBird’s quickstart script deploys the whole stack on one VM, and the project estimates about five minutes if you already have a domain and a server. Recent versions combine management, signal, relay, and STUN into a single container and include built-in user management, so you don’t need a separate identity provider just to log in.

This is definitely more than just a few clicks, though. You'll need a VPS with a public IP and a domain with proper DNS records pointing to it. The VPS can be of a very modest spec, because all it's really responsible for is authentication, presenting the web dashboard, and relaying traffic.

NetBird replaced Tailscale when I hit the 6-user limit, and it costs me $3 a month instead of $25

It used infrastructure I was already paying for

2
By  Ty Sherback

Start with NetBird's cloud deployment if you're just starting

If remote access is what’s standing between you and a home lab you can use from anywhere, NetBird Cloud is one of the fastest ways to get that done. Install the client, sign in, write a policy or two, and your services follow you wherever you go. If owning the control plane starts to matter to you, you can always move to the self-hosted version while using the same clients.

item.title: I tested Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, and it changed what I thought my 16GB GPU could do
item.itunes:title: I tested Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, and it changed what I thought my 16GB GPU could do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When it comes to local AI inference, I've treated my RTX 4070 Ti Super as a one-model-per-job card. As a matter of fact, I've also created an entire ensemble of models suited to a particular job that they do best, as I recently detailed last week, consisting of a research model, a coding model, and an image model. An agent that plans, browses, and acts on its own always felt like something that was exclusive to the most expensive cloud services, that is, until now.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Nvidia recently released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, which is a 74B model with 9B active parameters, built to fit in 24GB with native 2-bit weights. If you go through its model card right now, you'll find that every hardware configuration targets 32GB of memory or more, and it almost felt as though my 16GB card had no business running it. As stubborn as I am, I tried it anyway with nothing but my 16GB GPU, 32GB of RAM, and the right llama.cpp settings. Here's how it turned my gaming desktop into an RTX AI PC.

Getting a 74B model on a 16GB card took more than a download

My first attempt didn't make it past loading the file

Nvidia's official GGUF for the Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B stores every expert in IQ2_XXS quant, with the Mamba layers (a leaner alternative to attention layers) in NVFP4 and the attention layers in Q8_0. Along with the vision projector, the download was just under 24GB, which is already 8GB more than my 4070 Ti Super's VRAM.

The next challenge was that my existing llama.cpp build refused to load it. As it turns out, Bolt's experts are pruned differently from layer to layer, and older builds of llama.cpp reject that layout with a tensor shape error. As such, I had to move to build b11927, since the support for Bolt dropped on llama.cpp on the model's launch day.

Now, instead of guessing at how many expert layers my card could hold through trial-and-error with --n-cpu-moe, I let llama.cpp's --fit option work it out for me. After running the flag, llama.cpp filled my GPU to 15.7GB and left the rest in system memory. With all expert layers on the CPU, Bolt managed 19 tokens/second, and the fitted setup ran between 22–32 tokens per second, with prompt processing at 110 tokens/second.

Bolt also comes with LiLiCorr, which is a small companion model Nvidia trained to guess several words ahead so that the main model can check them in one go. Other model makers like Alibaba and Google have their own variant of it through multi-token prediction, but since LiLiCorr slowed things down on my card instead of speeding them up (as it took VRAM away from experts), speculative decoding went out the window.

For this test, I ran everything at 64K context with Nvidia's recommended sampler settings with a temperature of 1.0 and top_p of 0.95, along with llama.cpp's default sampler values of 40 for top_k and 0.05 for min_p.

I ran GLM 5.3, a 744-billion-parameter model, on my home lab, and the frontier suddenly feels a lot closer

1.5TB of model, 350GB of computer. Math shouldn't work like this.

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Getting Bolt to load was the first step, turning it into an agent was the next

Hermes Agent gave Bolt everything it needed

When I had the model running as it should via llama.cpp, it was time to see its agentic capabilities in action. Interestingly enough, Bolt's model card lists Hermes Agent reasoning traces in its post-training data, so it felt natural to pick it for the agent. I pointed it at my llama.cpp server as a custom endpoint and started the setup from a blank slate, enabling terminal, file access, vision, a local Chromium browser (for further tinkering later), memory, skills, and code execution. I left the cloud API key empty, as it wasn't necessary here.

I also deleted its 58 bundled skills, since two of them hand tasks to Claude Code and Codex, which could've silently sent work to the cloud. That would've been a problem for the experiment.

The first test I ran to check if everything was running as it should was pointing Bolt to a hardware monitor screenshot with 48 readings across CPU, GPU, and memory. Bolt's first attempt went a little sideways, but only because it trusted a folder listing it had run a few minutes earlier, decided the file didn't exist, and proceeded to spend the next two minutes searching the contents of files across my user folder for the file name. Thankfully, it didn't come up with invented values, which is something I feared.

I started a fresh session and gave it the full path in the next run. This time, it read all the 48 values correctly, including thousands separators, a 0 RPM fan minimum, and the log filename in the footer. The vision call took about 73 seconds, and the whole run was finished in 1 minute and 42 seconds.

I ran local LLMs on a "dead" GPU, and the results surprised me

My Pascal card may not be ideal for intensive workloads, but it's more than enough for light LLM-powered tasks

1
By  Ayush Pande

Then I made it do what Nvidia says it does best

I gave Bolt a multi-step job and didn't step in once

For the final test, I gave Bolt a five-step job, wherein it had to find the installed versions of llama.cpp and Hermes on my PC, check GitHub for their latest releases, dig up the pull request that added Bolt support to llama.cpp, write a report with sources, and save the method as a skill for the next time. I did not intervene in any part of the process, and it wrapped it up in 11 minutes and 44 seconds.

It first ran llama-cli to read my build number and pulled the Hermes version from the installed files. The browser took some time getting used to, and Bolt burned around eight tool calls figuring out how to read a page. item.title: Reliability Monitor has been in Windows since Vista, and it explains crashes better than Event Viewer ever will
item.itunes:title: Reliability Monitor has been in Windows since Vista, and it explains crashes better than Event Viewer ever will
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have been a Windows user for a long time, and I find the operating system incredibly convenient. Microsoft may have gone wrong with Windows on several occasions, but the overall experience still remains streamlined, at least it has for me. And one reason is that newer Windows iterations still include some of my favorite tools from the days of Vista and XP, even though few people use them.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It may come as a surprise, but I haven't used the Event Viewer to troubleshoot my computer in ages. It's not even the first tool I launch. I used it for a couple of years, until I came across Reliability Monitor. Initially shipped with Windows Vista, the tool has been a part of the Windows ecosystem ever since. Honestly, it has saved me countless hours that I would otherwise have spent digging through Event Viewer logs. Those logs, let's face it, can be pretty confusing for the average user.

Reliability Monitor's appeal lies in its simplicity

Quickly check your system's Stability Index

Imagine your system becoming incredibly slow, acting weird, or throwing errors. Unless you know what caused it, there's no point trying random fixes or applying age-old Windows advice. That's where the Reliability Monitor comes into the picture. It provides you with a simple, visual timeline of the important events. When you launch the utility, it will take a few seconds to generate a reliability report.

Once the interface loads, you will see all the important system events from the recent past. This includes installed and failed Windows updates, app crashes, service failures, and everything else that might be critical to your system. The best part is that the Reliability Monitor presents this information in a structured manner. You see a timeline where all the important events are highlighted. Critical events (those that generally require attention) are marked with red crosses; warnings or slightly non-critical problems are marked with the danger sign; and general events are marked with blue information icons. By default, the timeline shows you the day-by-day activity over the past 20 days, but you can switch to the Weeks view to check system activity over the past 20 weeks.

Personally, all this pales in comparison to what I like most about the Reliability Monitor: the Stability Index. The tool assigns your system a score on a scale of 1 to 10 based on its stability. The lower the score, the less stable your system is. Simply put, there were more hardware or software issues that particular day. So, you don't necessarily need to go through every event the Reliability Monitor registered. Just focus on days when the Stability Index dropped, and you will know what's wrong with the system or what's triggering those errors or slowdowns.

Most Event Viewer errors are normal, and you probably shouldn't be looking at them in the first place

Spend your time elsewhere

By  João Carrasqueira

It's a good starting point

You don't have to dig through countless logs

When it comes to troubleshooting, I check Reliability Monitor first, whether it's a program or the system as a whole. That's because it helps you identify the problem rather than forcing you to investigate, which alone saves a lot of time. You don't have to sift through hundreds of logs or filter them by importance. Everything that's important is right there in front of you, clearly highlighted and marked.

For more details about an event, double-click its entry in Reliability Monitor, and the tool will tell you what happened and, sometimes, the underlying cause too, like Event Viewer, but without all the extra information you don't need for basic troubleshooting. I find Reliability Monitor particularly helpful because it provides a clear timeline of important events that helps you connect the dots. When you know the sequence of events, it's much easier to connect the problem to a hardware or software change.

Let me give you an example. Recently, one of the applications that's critical to my workflow started crashing out of the blue. So I opened Reliability Monitor, reviewed how the crashes played out over the past week or so, and found they were linked to a particular DLL file. I know you could do the same using Event Viewer, but Reliability Monitor, frankly, makes troubleshooting a little fun.

5 built-in tools to use when troubleshooting Windows problems

You don't need third-party tools

2
By  Anurag Singh

Sometimes, Event Viewer is the better choice

It gives you more details

All that said, Event Viewer is sometimes the better choice, or even the only choice. While Reliability Monitor is good at a lot of things, some issues require you to get technical, and that's where Event Viewer shines. I agree. It's not one of the easiest tools to work with, especially for the average, everyday Windows user. But when it comes to digging deep into the events and generated logs, Event Viewer is my first choice.

Personally, I first check the Reliability Monitor, track my system's stability over the past week or since the problem appeared, and try to gather as much information as possible to identify the underlying cause. And if none of that helps, I turn to Event Viewer for detailed logs. A piece of advice: when using Event Viewer, always filter the logs, because the sheer volume can overwhelm the average user.

I had Claude look into my Windows 11 PC, and it revealed problems I didn’t know I had

"Hey Claude, what's wrong with my PC?"

3
By  Abhinav Raj

Reliability Monitor should get more attention

I am not entirely sure why the Reliability Monitor doesn't get as much attention, but it's certainly one of those forgotten Windows tools you should use more often. You can open the Reliability Monitor by searching for "View reliability history" or entering "perfmon /rel" in the Run command. The tool isn't just for troubleshooting the system. A quick check every few weeks will tell you how stable your system is and whether you missed any problems. It may not be the perfect solution or fix the problem for you, but it explains crashes better than Event Viewer ever has.

item.title: After only two years, Microsoft removes Copilot from all smart TVs
item.itunes:title: After only two years, Microsoft removes Copilot from all smart TVs
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Microsoft is ending Copilot support on all smart TVs, including LG models.
  • LG TVs show a notice that Copilot features will stop functioning sometime in 2026.
  • Microsoft is scaling back Copilot to focus on quality over rapid expansion.

Back at the turn of 2025, we saw the big announcement that Microsoft would be bringing its Copilot assistant to smart TVs. It was back when the company's game plan seemed to be to go wide and fast, establishing footholds in major tech channels before its competitors could.

However, it didn't seem to pan out, and Microsoft is now scaling back its Copilot rollout to focus on quality over quantity. A new message has reportedly appeared on LG TVs, announcing that the Redmond giant is removing Copilot from all smart TVs.

Microsoft is rolling back Copilot from all smart TVs

Not just LG TV ones

Za Bowden over on Windows Central first spotted this message while using his LG TV. It popped up from the side and informed him that the end of Copilot's time on his TV was nigh:

"We would like to inform you that Microsoft has recently decided to end support for Copilot functionality on all TVs, including the Copilot-enabled feature available on our LG TVs. As a result, the Copilot-enabled feature on your TV is no longer available and may stop functioning shortly."

Take special note of the wording in the first half of the first sentence. Microsoft isn't just pulling the plug on LG TVs: the statement claims it's ending support for "Copilot functionality on all TVs," which includes LG TVs. As such, we should see similar statements arrive from other smart TV manufacturers that adopted Copilot.

The message doesn't say the specific date when Copilot will lose support; all it says is that it should happen sometime in 2026. That gives people just a few months of use before it's gone for good, but I can't imagine too many people will be distraught by this change.

LG will finally let you remove the AI TV feature nobody asked for

It's here to stay

item.title: This PowerToys feature lets me move windows without touching the title bar, and now I can't go back
item.itunes:title: This PowerToys feature lets me move windows without touching the title bar, and now I can't go back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whether you're a Windows, Mac, or Linux user, you probably don't even think about the way you move windows around. After all, we've been doing it pretty much the same way for years. You click the title bar and drag the window wherever you want it. While this isn't necessarily a hassle, having to reach for the title bar every time I want to rearrange windows gets a little annoying, especially since I have two 27-inch monitors and a 34-inch ultrawide on my desk.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

As someone who's been using Windows for almost two decades, I never really questioned whether there was a better way to move windows. Even after I started using PowerToys recently for FancyZones and Command Palette, I never messed with it enough to realize it had a tool that could make dragging windows easier. Then, when I eventually came across the name "Grab And Move" in the list of utilities, curiosity got the better of me, so I decided to try it out. And now, I use it way more often than FancyZones.

I installed PowerToys for one feature, but these 3 tools made me keep it

Command Palette was just the gateway, I guess.

5
By  Hamlin Rozario

Grab And Move makes the title bar optional

I can now drag windows from practically anywhere inside them

Using Grab And Move is pretty simple. Just hold the modifier key (Alt by default) and drag anywhere inside the window with the left mouse button. That's it. You don't have to position your cursor over the title bar or look for an empty spot between the tabs in your browser. As long as you click somewhere inside the window, you can grab it and move it wherever you want. You can also change the modifier key to the Windows key if you'd rather not use Alt.

You can also exclude apps if you don't want Grab And Move interfering with their shortcuts or mouse controls. I haven't excluded anything myself, but if you have apps that use Alt in combination with mouse clicks, you may want to add them to the exclusions. By default, Grab And Move is disabled when Game Mode is on, so you don't have to worry about accidentally triggering it while playing first-person shooters. And none of this changes how you normally drag windows. You can still drag by the title bar if you want, but I haven't done that in weeks.

Resizing windows also gets an upgrade

You no longer need to drag from the edges or corners

Moving windows isn't the only thing Grab And Move has going for it. You can also resize them without having to position your cursor along their edges or corners. To resize a window, you need to use the right mouse button instead of the left one while holding down the same modifier key (Alt by default). You can drag from anywhere inside the window, and Grab And Move automatically determines which edge or corner to resize based on where you start dragging.

I'll admit this feature is a bit finicky compared to simply moving windows with Grab And Move. You still need to pay some attention to where you position your cursor, and sometimes, resizing diagonally can be a little tricky. I've had multiple instances where I wanted to adjust both the width and height of a window, only to end up resizing one side because I didn't start dragging close enough to the corner. Still, I'd much rather deal with this than reach for the edges or corners every time I want to resize.

It's not like Windows makes moving windows difficult

But this convenience is hard to give up now that I'm used to it

Windows may have a lot of problems, but I wouldn't necessarily count moving windows around as one of them. Dragging a window by its title bar is hardly a hassle, and we've been doing this for so many years without even thinking twice about it. Let's not forget that we now have Snap Layouts to quickly arrange multiple windows on our screens anyway. Not to mention keyboard shortcuts like Win + Left/Right Arrow for snapping a window to either side. So I get why you may think Grab And Move is mostly unnecessary.

But as someone who drags about a hundred windows in a day, that extra second I save by not reaching for the title bar surely adds up over time. I'm not saying Grab And Move has made me significantly more productive or anything like that, but it's the kind of convenience I notice every time I use my PC now. I've gotten so used to holding Alt that I don't even think about the title bar anymore. So if you spend a lot of time moving windows, I'd say Grab And Move is well worth trying. And if you don't like it, you can still drag the old-fashioned way.

A simple tool that I now use more than the ones I installed PowerToys for

I didn't think I needed a feature like this until I tried it, and I had no clue it would become one of my most-used PowerToys utilities. At this point, it's safe to say that Grab And Move has made me unlearn the traditional way of dragging windows. It's not like I can't go back to using the title bar, but why would I when I can just press an additional key and drag from anywhere inside the window? If anything, I just wish Microsoft would make this a native feature so I wouldn't have to keep PowerToys running in the background for something so basic.

It's almost like PowerToys exists to fix what Windows is lacking.

item.title: I turned off these 4 Android Auto settings, and my daily drives got a whole lot better
item.itunes:title: I turned off these 4 Android Auto settings, and my daily drives got a whole lot better
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Android Auto is essential for everyday navigation, streaming music in the car, and taking calls. It improves not just convenience, but in-car safety as well.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But some default settings can still be a bit more distracting than they should be. Whether it's messages interrupting navigation or the interface getting a bit more cluttered than I'd like, there's always room for improvement. Turns out, Android Auto gives you the tools to make those changes.

I've found that turning off a few of these features makes Android Auto much better suited to how I drive. I'm not losing any features here and still have access to navigation, calls, and all my favorite apps. But the fewer interruptions and more control go a long way towards improving my driving experience. Here are four Android Auto settings that I'd recommend changing the next time you're in your car.

Turn off messaging notifications

I prefer fewer message notifications while driving

My phone is the center of my digital life, which means that it also receives notifications all day long that can be pretty disruptive while driving. Most of these messages don't need an immediate response, but they still pull my attention off the road while I'm driving.

Android Auto can, obviously, display incoming message notifications on the car's screen. While this can be useful in many situations, in my city's stop-and-go traffic, it is more distracting than helpful. I've found it easier to stay focused on the road by turning off the Show Message Notifications setting. Go to Settings on your phone, search for Android Auto, scroll down, and turn off Show Message Notifications.

The obvious trade-off is that I no longer get a message when a notification arrives. But when on the road, that's not a big miss, and I can always open the messaging app and check for incoming texts there when I'm parked.

I turned off these Android Auto features, and my driving experience got so much better

A calmer dashboard changed everything

3
By  Parth Shah

Turn off the conversation chime

Why message alerts interrupt my driving experience

Visual interruptions are one thing, but Android Auto also plays an audible alert anytime a message comes in. To me, this is just as distracting, because it makes me think something needs my attention. Not only that, but these conversation chimes also interrupt when I'm listening to music, a podcast, or an audiobook.

When I say I don't want communication-related interruptions, I mean all kinds. That's why I've also disabled the conversation chime. To change it, just open Android Auto's Settings on your phone and look for the Conversation Chime option under Messaging Settings. Disable it to turn off the alert. The available options may vary depending on your software version.

Turn off automatic music playback

I prefer curating my driving playlist

Music is a huge part of my driving ritual. It involves pulling up the right playlist for the right mood. With autumn coming in, my current rotation includes a selection of Black Metal classics. Android Auto, on the other hand, starts playing whatever was last playing. This could be a random song on YouTube or Spotify.

It's disruptive, but more than that, just plain annoying. I get why some people like the feature. If you just want something to play with when you start your car, it works well enough, but it's not for me.

Disabling automatic playback gives me that choice. Android Auto obviously still lets me open my streaming app of choice, or even a local-music app like Symfonium. I can then select whatever I want to queue up and have it in my car's infotainment system. It's as easy as that. As it turns out, changing the setting is pretty simple.

Open Android Auto's Settings on your phone and scroll to the Start Music Automatically option. Next, toggle it Off. In most cases, that switches off the behavior. If your car still resumes music playback, your infotainment system might have its own music-resume setting you can toggle off.

Turn off taskbar widgets

Why I prefer a less cluttered Android Auto screen

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Android Auto can display quick controls in the taskbar that let you access media and navigation functions without leaving the app you're in. It's useful, but personally, I prefer a less cluttered interface. More importantly, my car's infotainment system is relatively small compared to the 14-inch or larger displays some cars come with these days.

For me, the taskbar is already enough. It gives you access to apps and other controls, and I rarely need extra widgets. If you don't mind dipping into the app drawer to switch between apps, turning off the Show Taskbar Widgets option can be a good trade-off for a simpler interface. It's a matter of personal preference, of course.

The setting isn't hard to find. Just tap the Show Taskbar Widgets option under Android Auto Settings, and you're good to go. If you miss the widgets, it's easy to get them back.

Customize Android Auto to suit your driving habits

Android Auto's beauty is its flexibility. It's not that I don't appreciate all these features. It's just that they don't fit in with how I use my phone.

Being able to turn off the features I don't like is a big part of why I enjoy using Android Auto. None of these changes will be essential to every driver. But for me, the best setup stays focused on driving, and turning off these options lets me build a setup geared specifically toward that.
